pos: n. pl. (the family of Shelah, numbered among the tribes of Israel)
etymology: Hebrew ha-Shelani, the Shelanite, a patronymic from Shelah, from the proper name Shelah, a petition or a sprout; named once, Numbers 26:20.
biblical_def: The Shelanites are the family of Shelah, Judah's third son by the daughter of Shua: “And the sons of Judah after their families were; of Shelah, the family of the Shelanites: of Pharez, the family of the Pharzites: of Zerah, the family of the Zarhites” (Numbers 26:20). Shelah is the son Judah withheld from Tamar, which is how Pharez and Zerah came to be born at all. “And she yet again conceived, and bare a son; and called his name Shelah: and he was at Chezib, when she bare him” (Genesis 38:5). The register in Genesis keeps the whole account: “And the sons of Judah; Er, and Onan, and Shelah, and Pharez, and Zerah: but Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan” (Genesis 46:12). Two of Judah's five sons were struck down for wickedness, one was withheld in fear, and the line of Messiah came through the twins born of a disgraceful episode. Four centuries later the Shelanites are counted in the plains of Moab as a family of Israel with a share in the land, no part of that history denied and no part of it holding them back.

corruption_summary: Shameful family origins are expected to be buried or explained away; Numbers 26 counts Judah's houses and Genesis 38 is still in the Bible.
corruption_paragraphs: The genealogy of Judah is not respectable. Er was wicked and the LORD slew him; Onan was wicked and the LORD slew him; Judah withheld Shelah; Tamar played the harlot to obtain by deceit what justice had denied her. Scripture narrates all of it, names the children, and then counts their descendants by family in the wilderness census with no asterisk attached.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's sovereign purposes run through histories that He Himself condemns, without any pretence that they were not sinful. Matthew keeps the same record in the genealogy of Christ: “And Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar” (Matthew 1:3). The Shelanites were numbered in Israel on the plain of Moab, and their family name is a standing testimony that God does not need a clean family tree to keep a promise.

pos: n. pl. (the family of Pharez, numbered among the tribes of Israel)
etymology: Hebrew ha-Partsi, the Pharzite, a patronymic from Pharez, from the proper name Pharez, a breach or a breaking forth; named once, Numbers 26:20.
biblical_def: The Pharzites are the family of Pharez, the elder of Tamar's twins: “And the sons of Judah after their families were; of Shelah, the family of the Shelanites: of Pharez, the family of the Pharzites: of Zerah, the family of the Zarhites” (Numbers 26:20). The name was given at the birth, when the midwife had bound a scarlet thread on the hand that came out first and the other child broke through ahead of him. Pharez means a breach. From this family came Hezron, Ram, Amminadab, Nahshon, Salmon, Boaz, Obed, Jesse and David, and from David the Lord Jesus Christ. In the census of Numbers 26 none of that is visible; the Pharzites are simply one family among the five of Judah, counted with the rest so that the land might be apportioned. “Unto these the land shall be divided for an inheritance according to the number of names” (Numbers 26:53). The royal line is in the list without any mark on it.

corruption_summary: A census treats every household alike; the family through which Messiah would come is counted in Numbers 26 with no distinction whatever.
corruption_paragraphs: It would be natural to expect the messianic line to be flagged in the registers, and it never is. The Pharzites appear between the Shelanites and the Zarhites, numbered and apportioned, with nothing to indicate that the covenant promise to Judah ran through them. The distinction was real and entirely hidden.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God works His largest purposes without advertisement, through families that look like every other family in the list. “Notwithstanding the land shall be divided by lot: according to the names of the tribes of their fathers they shall inherit” (Numbers 26:55). The breach that gave Pharez his name became, in time, the line of the King.

pos: n. pl. (the family of Pua, numbered among the tribes of Israel)
etymology: Hebrew ha-Puni, the Punite, a patronymic from Pua, from the proper name Pua or Puvah, a mouth or utterance; named once, Numbers 26:23.
biblical_def: The Punites are one of the four families of Issachar: “Of the sons of Issachar after their families: of Tola, the family of the Tolaites: of Pua, the family of the Punites” (Numbers 26:23). Pua is the second son of Issachar, named in Genesis and again in Chronicles, and the family is given no story beyond its numbering. What the chapter is doing with such families is stated twice: “Take the sum of all the congregation of the children of Israel, from twenty years old and upward, throughout their fathers' house, all that are able to go to war in Israel” (Numbers 26:2), and “Unto these the land shall be divided for an inheritance according to the number of names” (Numbers 26:53). The same count served two purposes: who would fight for the land, and who would receive it. A family too small to have a story in Scripture still had both obligations and a portion.

corruption_paragraphs: Numbers 26 counts families of widely different size and treats them identically in principle: every one musters its men of twenty years and upward, and every one inherits according to the number of its names. A family with no narrative in Scripture had precisely the same standing before the law as one with a chapter to itself.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the covenant obligations and the covenant blessings run to every household in the people of God, not to the prominent ones. The Punites fought for a land they would help divide, and their one verse in the Bible records both.

pos: n. pl. (the family of Jachin, numbered among the tribes of Israel)
etymology: Hebrew ha-Yakini, the Jachinite, a patronymic from Jachin, from the proper name Jachin, he will establish; named once, Numbers 26:12.
biblical_def: The Jachinites are a family of Simeon: “The sons of Simeon after their families: of Nemuel, the family of the Nemuelites: of Jamin, the family of the Jaminites: of Jachin, the family of the Jachinites” (Numbers 26:12). The name Jachin means he will establish, and it is the name later given to one of the two pillars Solomon set up in the porch of the temple. Simeon's numbering in this census is the sharpest reversal in the chapter: at Sinai the tribe had mustered fifty-nine thousand three hundred; in the plains of Moab it musters twenty-two thousand two hundred, a loss of more than half, while most tribes held or grew. The reason is not stated here, though the plague at Baal-peor, where a prince of Simeon was slain in the act of sin, stands a chapter earlier. A family named he will establish belonged to the tribe that came nearest to being extinguished.

corruption_summary: Numbers are read as neutral data; set side by side, the two censuses of Israel tell a moral history the narrative never states outright.
corruption_paragraphs: Nothing in Numbers 26 comments on Simeon. The verdict is in the arithmetic: fifty-nine thousand three hundred at Sinai, twenty-two thousand two hundred at Moab. The reader who has just read chapter 25, where Zimri the son of Salu, a prince of a chief house among the Simeonites, was slain with the Midianitish woman, is left to draw the line himself.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's judgments are often written in outcomes rather than announcements, and that a people's decline can be the loudest sermon in the book. The family of he will establish survived, and Simeon entered the land, but diminished.

pos: n. pl. (the family of Shaul, numbered among the tribes of Israel)
etymology: Hebrew ha-Sha'uli, the Shaulite, a patronymic from Shaul, from the proper name Shaul, asked or demanded; named once, Numbers 26:13.
biblical_def: The Shaulites close the list of Simeon's families: “Of Zerah, the family of the Zarhites: of Shaul, the family of the Shaulites” (Numbers 26:13). Shaul is named in Genesis with a detail the registers do not usually give: he was “the son of a Canaanitish woman” (Genesis 46:10). A son born to Simeon by a woman of the land, in the generation that went down into Egypt, becomes a reckoned family of Israel four centuries later, mustered for war and apportioned a share of Canaan. The notice is not an accusation; it is simply recorded, as Scripture records the Egyptian wife of Joseph and the Moabitess Ruth. The tribe as a whole had been halved by this census, and this family stood in the remnant. The name means asked, from the same root as the name of Israel's first king and of the apostle Paul before his was changed.

corruption_paragraphs: Shaul's mother is identified as a Canaanitess in Genesis 46 and never mentioned again. The Chronicler repeats the pedigree without the detail. The family is numbered, mustered, apportioned and left alone. Neither the modern instinct to make descent definitive nor the opposite instinct to pretend it was not written is supported by the text.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that membership in the covenant people rests on God's calling and the covenant sign, not on the purity of a bloodline. Rahab and Ruth were brought in; Achan of Judah was cut off. “For they are not all Israel, which are of Israel” (Romans 9:6).

pos: n. pl. (one of the three families of scribes that dwelt at Jabez, of the Kenites)
etymology: Hebrew Tir'athim, gate-dwellers, or those who blow the horn, of uncertain root; named once, 1 Chronicles 2:55.
biblical_def: The Tirathites are named in one of the most unusual verses in the genealogies: “And the families of the scribes which dwelt at Jabez; the Tirathites, the Shimeathites, and Suchathites. These are the Kenites that came of Hemath, the father of the house of Rechab” (1 Chronicles 2:55). Three things are stated at once. These are families of scribes — hereditary houses of men who could read and write and copy. They lived at Jabez, a town otherwise unknown. And they were Kenites, which is to say not Israelites by blood at all, but of the people of Jethro, who had attached themselves to Israel at the exodus and kept faith ever after. The verse ends by linking them to Rechab, whose sons Jeremiah would later commend for keeping their father's command when Judah would not keep God's. The men who copied Israel's books were, in part, the descendants of Gentile allies who had come in from the wilderness.

corruption_summary: Literacy and the keeping of texts are credited to institutions; in Israel they ran in families, and in this case in families of Gentile origin.
corruption_paragraphs: A people's Scriptures are preserved by somebody, and Chronicles tells us who: hereditary houses of scribes living in one town. That the Holy Ghost identifies them as Kenites is more striking still. The Kenites came up out of the wilderness with Israel — “And the children of the Kenite, Moses' father in law, went up out of the city of palm trees with the children of Judah” (Judges 1:16) — and never assimilated out of recognition.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God brings in strangers and gives them real work in His house. The Rechabites of this stock were held up by Jeremiah as a rebuke to Judah: “Jonadab the son of Rechab shall not want a man to stand before me for ever” (Jeremiah 35:19). Their kinsmen kept the text.

pos: n. pl. (one of the three families of scribes that dwelt at Jabez, of the Kenites)
etymology: Hebrew Sukhathim, bush-dwellers, or those of the thicket, from a root signifying a booth or covert; named once, 1 Chronicles 2:55.
biblical_def: The Suchathites stand third in the same verse: “And the families of the scribes which dwelt at Jabez; the Tirathites, the Shimeathites, and Suchathites. These are the Kenites that came of Hemath, the father of the house of Rechab” (1 Chronicles 2:55). Their name appears to mean dwellers in booths or thickets, which fits a people of tent-dwelling origin who had not wholly left their manner of life behind. The surrounding verses are about the towns of Judah and the households that founded them — “The sons of Salma; Bethlehem, and the Netophathites, Ataroth, the house of Joab, and half of the Manahethites, the Zorites” (1 Chronicles 2:54) — so the scribes of Jabez are placed among the settled families of Judah, though their descent is traced elsewhere. Scripture records them in a single clause and tells us nothing more. The copying of the sacred text in Israel was in the hands of men whose names survive only here.

corruption_paragraphs: Modern accounts of how the Old Testament came down to us begin with schools, traditions and institutions. Chronicles begins with three households in a town called Jabez. The record is concrete where the theories are abstract, and it attaches the work to actual families whose other distinction was that their fathers had come in with Israel out of Midian.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the ordinary, traceable providence by which God has kept His word. The Kenites pitched their tents on the edges of Israel for centuries — “Now Heber the Kenite, which was of the children of Hobab the father in law of Moses, had severed himself from the Kenites” (Judges 4:11) — and some of them sat down at Jabez and copied Scripture.

pos: n. pl. (a family reckoned among the sons of Salma, in the towns of Judah)
etymology: Hebrew ha-Tsor'i, the Zorite, a gentilic apparently from Zorah, a place of hornets; named once, 1 Chronicles 2:54.
biblical_def: The Zorites close a verse listing the townships founded by one household: “The sons of Salma; Bethlehem, and the Netophathites, Ataroth, the house of Joab, and half of the Manahethites, the Zorites” (1 Chronicles 2:54). The list mixes people and places in the Hebrew manner, because in this chapter a father and a town are the same kind of thing: Salma is called the father of Bethlehem, and the households that spread out from him became the villages of that part of Judah. Bethlehem itself stands first in the verse, four centuries before David and a thousand before the birth of Christ, reckoned as one of the settlements of a family in a genealogy. The Zorites take their name, most probably, from Zorah, the town of Manoah and Samson in the lowland of Judah. Nothing further is said of them. Their one verse does what the whole chapter does: it shows how a tribe became a landscape.

corruption_paragraphs: A modern reader stumbles over a verse that lists Bethlehem and the Netophathites in the same breath as though both were sons. The Hebrew genealogies are not confused; they are recording that households became settlements. “Salma the father of Bethlehem, Hareph the father of Bethgader” (1 Chronicles 2:51) is the same idiom.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's dealings with His people take root in soil. The covenant was with families, and the families became towns, and one of those towns in this verse is where the Son of God was born. Zorah down the valley gave Israel Samson: “And there was a certain man of Zorah, of the family of the Danites, whose name was Manoah” (Judges 13:2).

pos: n. pl. (a company of men of Judah who dwelt at Jerusalem after the captivity)
etymology: Hebrew ha-Shiloni, the Shilonite, taken either from Shiloh the town or as a form of Shelanite, the family of Shelah; named once in this plural, 1 Chronicles 9:5.
biblical_def: The Shilonites appear in a single short verse in the roll of those who resettled Jerusalem: “And of the Shilonites; Asaiah the firstborn, and his sons” (1 Chronicles 9:5). The surrounding verses set the scene: “And in Jerusalem dwelt of the children of Judah, and of the children of Benjamin, and of the children of Ephraim, and Manasseh” (1 Chronicles 9:3). The name is read two ways. Some take it from Shiloh, the town in Ephraim where the tabernacle stood for generations; others read it as a variant of Shelanite, the family of Shelah the son of Judah, since the company is listed among the children of Judah. The second is the likelier, and if so these are the descendants of the Shelanites numbered in the plains of Moab, now back from Babylon and living in the ruined capital. Either way the verse does what Chronicles always does at this point: it names who came back, and whose sons they were.

corruption_summary: A name with two possible derivations is treated as evidence of textual confusion; the honest course is to state both readings and claim neither as certain.
corruption_paragraphs: Where the Hebrew admits two readings, pressure runs toward asserting one with a confidence the evidence does not supply. Shilonite may mean a man of Shiloh or a descendant of Shelah. The context among the children of Judah favours the second. That is as far as the text takes us, and a dictionary that pretends further is not serving its reader.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is honesty about the limits of what is revealed, which is a form of reverence rather than a concession. Chronicles' purpose here is not etymological: “So all Israel were reckoned by genealogies; and, behold, they were written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah” (1 Chronicles 9:1). Asaiah the firstborn and his sons came back, and that is what the verse is for.

pos: n. (the villages of Netophah, home of the singers who kept the dedication of the wall)
etymology: Hebrew Netophathi, of Netophah, from nataph, to drop or distil, as of dew or myrrh; named once in this form, Nehemiah 12:28.
biblical_def: Netophathi is named at the gathering for the dedication of the wall: “And the sons of the singers gathered themselves together, both out of the plain country round about Jerusalem, and from the villages of Netophathi” (Nehemiah 12:28). Nehemiah had sought the Levites out of all their places “to keep the dedication with gladness, both with thanksgivings, and with singing, with cymbals, psalteries, and with harps” (Nehemiah 12:27), and the singers had to be fetched in from the countryside, because “the singers had builded them villages round about Jerusalem” (Nehemiah 12:29). Netophah lay near Bethlehem; its name comes from a root meaning to drop or distil, used of dew and of sweet gum. What followed was one of the loudest days in the Old Testament: two great companies of singers on the wall, going opposite ways around the city, meeting in the house of God. “Also that day they offered great sacrifices, and rejoiced: for God had made them rejoice with great joy: the wives also and the children rejoiced: so that the joy of Jerusalem was heard even afar off” (Nehemiah 12:43).

corruption_summary: Corporate praise is treated as atmosphere; at the dedication of the wall it was organised, rehearsed, funded, and loud enough to be heard outside the city.
corruption_paragraphs: Nehemiah's dedication is the opposite of spontaneous. Levites were sought out of all their places and brought in; singers were fetched from Netophah and the plain country; two great companies were appointed, with Ezra at the head of one and Nehemiah behind the other; instruments were specified. The joy was deliberate, and it was worked at.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God is to be praised with ordered, costly, corporate worship, and that the ordering does not quench the gladness but produces it. The result was not a mood but a sound: the joy of Jerusalem heard even afar off, by neighbours who had spent three months trying to stop the work.
